title: Spatiotemporal programming via asymmetric dielectric engineering for nonvolatile 2D optoelectronics
authors: Xiaoguang Luo, Xiaolong Zhang, Honglei Chen, Jiaming Wang, Fan Liu, Jiongtao Zhang, Junqiang Zhang, Yihan Yin, Jinpeng Xu, Lei Ying, Renjing Xu, Yingchun Cheng, Xuetao Gan, Wei Huang
abstract: Ambipolar two dimensional (2D) semiconductors integrated with floating-gate architectures offer a promising platform for nonvolatile, reconfigurable electronics. However, the switching between p-n and n-p junction polarities has conventionally required complex multi-gate designs, hindering the scalability and integration density. Here, we demonstrate a spatiotemporal programming strategy using a dual-floating-gate architecture with a symmetry broken tunneling dielectric. An asymmetric dielectric stack creates distinct tunneling thresholds for two floating gates, enabling a single input gate to encode spatial doping profiles in the 2D channel via defined voltage pulse sequences. We achieve on demand, nonvolatile, and reversible switching between p-n and n-p configurations with excellent retention and endurance. The reconfigurable homojunction serves as a multifunctional platform for logic encoding, rectification, photodetection, and in sensor computing. This work establishes a design paradigm that replaces spatial input complexity with spatiotemporal programming, paving the way for high-density, multifunctional intelligent hardware.
summary: This work presents a novel dual-floating-gate 2D optoelectronic device capable of nonvolatilely programming its junction polarity and optical response using spatiotemporal gate pulses. The device is shown to function as a versatile platform for rectifying signals, harvesting power, and critically, implementing artificial neural networks directly within the sensor chip for enhanced robustness.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for nonvolatile, reconfigurable electronic platforms capable of performing multiple functions like logic encoding, rectification, and photodetection on demand.
main_result: A dual-floating-gate architecture using 2D semiconductors enables spatiotemporal programming to achieve reversible p-n/n-p switching and high-performance in-sensor artificial neural network computation.
method: The authors combine electrical characterization (I-V curves, transfer characteristics) with optical measurements (photocurrent mapping) and machine learning simulation (ANN training/quantization).
model_or_system: The core system is a dual-floating-gate (DFG) device built on 2D semiconductors (MoTe2), utilizing a symmetry-broken tunneling dielectric stack for programming. This structure allows for the creation of stable, nonvolatile homojunctions.
key_observables: Polarity switching ratio ($\sim 10^4$), responsivity (R), power conversion efficiency ($\eta_{PCE}$), and ANN classification accuracy (up to 87.50%).
important_parameters: Gate-voltage pulse sequences (e.g., (60, –30) V), incident laser power density ($P_{in}$), and the discrete programmable states defining synaptic weights.
main_assumptions: The asymmetry in the dielectric stack is assumed to be due to non-uniform tunneling paths, and the ANN performance relies on the quantization of weights into these discrete physical states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate device schematics, band structures, output characteristics showing p-n/n-p switching, photocurrent mapping confirming homojunctions, and transfer curves demonstrating memory windows.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating basic nonvolatile switching and rectification to characterizing photovoltaic performance, and finally applying the device's programmable photoresponse to implement and test an in-sensor ANN for action classification.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the integration of physical device states (the discrete memory windows) to emulate quantized synaptic weights for machine learning places it at the intersection of physical modeling and computational physics, relevant to understanding emergent behavior in complex systems.
